speaker: Speaker 1
words: The following interview is of Mamie Reeser recorded at St. Mary's, Idaho July 14, 1975 by Dale Anderson. First of all, just some personal information and then we get into the questions. But if you want to say anything in between, go ahead.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, your name? Mamie Reeser. Is that your real name or nickname?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My real name is Mary, but they've always called me Mamie and everybody knows me by Mamie. M-A-M-I-E.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mottr, M-O-T-T-E-R-N.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Reeser, R-E-S-O-R. Okay, got that. Your date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: August 7th, 1914.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 1914? Uh-huh. You don't look that old at all. Your place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Trummer, Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Locale for Christmas, that was Plummer. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you know where Plummer is?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I've been through Plummer. Uh-huh. Okay. I'm going to take care of all those questions since you were here all the time. Your mother's maiden name? Sally.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Kavanagh. C-A-V-A-N-A-U-G-H.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My mother's name is Ella.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was it really? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I haven't heard that many people named Ella.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have a new granddaughter that's a month old tomorrow and her middle name is Ella. They named her after my mother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's really nice. Some friends of mine adopted a little girl and her middle name is Ella and it stands for my mother and her grandmother. So that works out nicely. The date of her birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: February the 1st, 1874.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Romeo, Michigan. Romeo?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Michigan. Date of death?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh dear. Well I know it was, let's see, August 1961.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She was married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Her occupations and jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh my, lots of them. She was a school teacher and she was a, um, she had a hat shop and she was, had a cafe and she was a midwife and a half wife.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And a homesteader.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did she first come to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, probably around 1900. Because she had her homestead on Marble Creek before she was ever married and she was married in 1908.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she come out here, did she come out with her family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, she came out with her father on Marble Creek. I'll tell you when she came out, she was 18 years old. So how old would that make her? She was born 1874 and 18, she came out...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay, that's when she came out here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And she, it was just her and her father that came out of the home? Uh-huh, uh-huh. Your father's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Edwin Modern.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The date of his birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: December the 9th. No, 7th. December the 7th, 1873.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The place of his birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Knoxville, Tennessee.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the day of his death? Uh...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Hmm, let's see, it was 1960.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: His occupations and jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh dear. Well, he was mostly a lumberjack.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Was he also a homesteader or just a lumberjack? Well...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I would say mostly a lumberjack. He did a lot of odd jobs, but I think mainly he was a lumberjack.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know how your parents met? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They met in Harrison. My mother had a cafe in Harrison. And his family moved from the Rockford Reservation. When he came from Tennessee, they settled on the Rockford Reservation, which it wasn't even a county or a city or a state that called it the reservation. It was an Indian reservation at Rockford. And then they went from there to Harrison.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He met in Harrison. Okay. Your brothers and sisters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have two brothers only, and one of them is Joe B. Modern.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And the other one is John H. Modern.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your husband's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Stanley L. Reesor.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: October the 17th, 1908. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Phillipsburg, Kansas.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The date and place you were married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: August the 22nd, Colorado Springs, Colorado.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you wind up getting married in Colorado Springs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Stanley went into the service. And he was in the Army Infantry during World War II in Colorado. And I went down there. And I went down there and was married down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did you know him before you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Probably ten years, off and on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, did you know him in high school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Knew him, well, really not in school, but I knew him after school. You know, after I got out of school and after he was out of school. I remember him in school, but I didn't know him all that well.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long were you actually courting?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Probably five or six years. Off and on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was the year?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That we were married? 1942?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I got married in Pueblo. Okay. Your husband's occupation and job?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He has a pool hall downtown. And before that he worked for the Forest Service.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you didn't have any children, is that right? Oh, you do, when?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh, I have two children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Their names?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Andrew John Reeser.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was going to say, wait a minute, we're talking about it. Just a minute ago, I was thinking, there's somebody I called who said they didn't have any children. And I was thinking it was you. No. Okay. And the date and place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay, he was born September the 28th, 1943, in Colorado.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: His occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's an accountant with the Boeing Company in Seattle.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I have a daughter, Candice Sue Reeser Pugh, P-U-G-H.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Date and place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And she was born March the 22nd, 1949, in St. Mary's.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And her occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She took, she majored in Home Ec at the university and she's a home, she took Extension work. And she works with the Benewalt County Extension Office, County Agent's Office, part-time. And she's also a clerk with me at Davidson Lane, part-time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have a grandchild?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh, a new one, a month old tomorrow.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's right. Is that hers?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. And Andy has two. I have three granddaughters.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, are they both in town? No. Wait, he's in town, she's in town. I haven't started listening yet. Okay, any other? Not yet. Okay, your education?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm just a high school graduate, St. Mary's High School.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long have you lived in St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Since 1927.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your skill?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I'm a clerk. A buyer and a clerk.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, where did you say you live?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Davidson Lane.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Davidson Lane?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Lane, uh-huh, it's a clothing store.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, your interest, how do you can tell? Well,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm a lawyer. I've belonged to the American Legion Auxiliary since about 1945. And I have worked with it and I have worked with, I worked with the Sringer Girls State for about seven years and I was state director in 1962.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, any fans?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, oh, I've belonged to various organizations in town, but that's about all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are they?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Eastern Star. And the American Legion Auxiliary in 8th and 4th.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 8th and 4th?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 8th and 4th. It's 8ET40.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Awards, honors, and rhythms.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the only thing, I got, I received an award when I was Dan Mother for the Cub Scout, that's the only...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, have you ever entered anything in the county fair? No. Any other hobbies or interests?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I think that's all. Okay. What's your favorite song?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think it would be nice just to kind of do a rundown of your life, just go through the history.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was born in Plummer and I lived there and went through the fifth grade.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type of school was it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just a small school, just a small, you know, it was all grades, but it was, you know, it wasn't a large school. And then in 1927 I moved to St. Mary's and I went to school here. And I was active in school activities. I mean, I was, you know, worked with the annual and was in the school. I was the pep club, I was pep club president one year. And then I started work at Robeson's, it was a clothing store, and I worked there for, let's see, I think it was six years. And then I was a telephone operator for a couple years and then I worked at JCPenney for two years just before I was married. And then I went to Colorado and was married and we lived in Colorado and at Fort Lewis, Washington until after the war. We came home in 1945 from Fort Lewis, Washington. My husband guarded the German prisons at Fort Lewis. And then we came home in 1945 and I've lived here ever since. And while the children were small, I worked with the Cub Scout program and the girl, Camper Girls. And Andy was in the rifle club and the 4-H club and I helped him with those things. And Candy was in the campfire and I was the leader all through Bluebirds in campfire until I think the last year that she was in campfire. I wasn't her leader. And during this time I was busy with the American Legion Auxiliary and for a number of years I was a Rebecca but I dropped out later because I never attended. But in my early years, before I was married, I belonged to the Rebecca Lodge and I went through the chairs before I was married in the Rebecca Lodge. And then I started to work in 1959 at Davis Link to help the children through college and both Andy and Candy have graduated from the University of Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you and your husband expect Andy to go to school? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I, when Andy was born, we took out an endowment for him so that he could go to college. And the first year he went, he went to the College of Idaho in Caldwell because I had worked for seven years in Caldwell with Girls State and so I wanted him to start school down there. So the first year we sent him to the College of Idaho and then the next year he transferred to the University. And he graduated with a degree in accounting and he went to work that following November for Boeing. This is my husband, Mr. Eason.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Nice to meet you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Would you like to have a shot of wine or something?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Thank you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And he's been with the Boeing Company for the last nine years. And then Candy went two years to the junior college in Coeur d'Alene and then transferred to the University and graduated down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your parents expect for you to go to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My mother always wanted me to be a schoolteacher because she was a schoolteacher. But when I graduated from high school, it was 1932 and it was during the Depression. And there was very little money to be had or around. And when I went to work at the store downtown, everyone said, well, you're just as well off, you have a job. And that's as well as not, so I never did go on to college. But my mother always wanted me to be a schoolteacher.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you want to be a nurse?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sort of, sort of. But I knew there wouldn't be enough money to put me through school. And at that time, there isn't opportunities that there is now for children to go to school and work. You know, there just wasn't those opportunities at that time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did your mother teach you to tell?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm not sure. She taught in Minnesota. And I don't think it was too long. But I know I did have a picture of her and she said they called her the kid schoolteacher because she had natural curly hair and she had this long curl and she said they called her the kid schoolteacher. She was a remarkable woman, my mother was. She was really something. She first came to Lewiston and then they came up to me. And then they came up to Harrison and Coeur d'Alene. And she homesteaded at Marble Creek when she was just a young girl. And she kept her saddle pony at what was then Farrell. There isn't anything now. But there was a family there that kept her horse. And then she would go twice a year from Coeur d'Alene or Harrison to Farrell and then ride her horse up to Marble Creek and twelve miles into the mountain to keep her homestead. All by herself. She was just a young girl then.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did she do that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I'm not sure about that either. She had it until after she was married, I know. She probably had it for probably, I would say probably six years, maybe five or six years, that she kept her homestead.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did they sell it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, she could have but she didn't. She let my father log it with a partner and it wasn't successful. She should have sold it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the land go in the family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How far was Marble Creek? Was it actually on the creek or was it near that station?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, it was, I think it was on Eagle Creek. As near as I can remember. I was up there when I was just a small child. We spent one summer up there. And lived in her cabin that she had made when I was just a little girl. And as I remember, it was on Eagle Creek was where her claim was, her homestead.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How about the cabin, did she... She did. That's great. When you were born, what, were you born in a hospital?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I was born at home with a midwife, but I don't even know who it was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what about when you had your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They were both born in hospitals.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you learn about childbearing and raising?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well... Just my own experience, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you were pregnant, did you ask your doctor a lot of questions?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not really, I don't think. Of course, the first one I had was in Colorado. And... Nothing out of the ordinary, I mean, just your usual questions, you know, weight and so forth.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It wasn't all that great.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are some of the advantages and disadvantages of living in a rural area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of course, I've always lived in a small town. Except when we were in Colorado and on the coast, and of course I prefer a small town. Always. I think you know more people. Um... I... We enjoyed Colorado, and I liked it much better than I did when we lived in Fort Lewis. But I don't like living in a large town. I didn't then. People aren't friendly, they aren't sociable like they are in a small place. You don't have the friends or the social contacts that you do in a small place.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you notice any changes in the family through the town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, St. Mary's is growing and it's different. There's new people. It isn't like it was 20 years ago. Because 20 years ago we knew everybody.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, you know, you knew practically everybody in town. And now there's so many new people and strange people that it's different.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the things that you did when you were a child?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, like what?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Recreation.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, well, of course we swam. And I played tennis.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of course at that time we all, during the winter, we always had our sleds and went coasting, which they don't do now. And they swam, but we always swam in the rivers, up and down the rivers. And now they have approval. And I think that's about all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did your children do for recreation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well... Of course Andy was always real active in all his, like, 4-H and rifle club. And...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: coasted and went ice skating and... and some swimming, not a great deal, but he did some. And he played ball.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Um...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Candy never swam. But, um, she was in 4-H and Bluebirds. And she took a few dancing lessons when she was little. I gave her dancing lessons.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was funny. She had her girlfriends and they played back and forth.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was fun. Okay. What are some of the things that you remember about your courtship and early married life? Well...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't remember too much about my courtship except that we went to dances and shows and things like that, you know. I mean, we were always... We went to Spokane lots and attended lots of dances and shows. And down at Chattcolat Lake they had dances and we used to go down there. But then when I was married I was in Colorado, you see, and... We spent... Well, I was there from 42 until... I went down in August of 42 and I was there until...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Probably December. No. Yes, December of 43. When I came home. And... We enjoyed that because we did a lot of touring on the weekends. We went to all the sightseeing places in Colorado. I enjoyed that. You know, to the Garden of the Gods, the Broadmoor Hotel. And we attended Sunrise Service, in fact, when we were there at the Garden of the Gods. And that was when Camp Carson was full of soldiers and the airport had the... airport there and they all attended... A lot of the soldiers attended the Sunrise Service and it was real nice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where's some of the other places that you went to see in Colorado?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We went to Pueblo. We went to Will Rogers Shrine and the zoo several times and that was real interesting. And I understand now Norad's under Cheyenne Mountain. And we went to Pikes Peak. We went to Pikes Peak. There was a lot of things to see and a lot of things to do in Colorado which we didn't have around here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Especially right around Colorado Springs. Right. Did you ever go to Mesa Verde? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Lots of Sundays we went out to Manitou Springs. Have you ever been out there?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, I have been in Manitou Springs.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Lots of Sundays. They had... It was sort of like a carnival type place and we went out there... Oh, any number of Sundays we spent the day.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you go through Rocky Mountain National Park? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We went through Yellowstone Park when I went down. But just crossed through it was all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yellowstone, Colorado for two summers. I traveled around a bit over here to see Colorado. I did. What were some of the reasons that you got married? In other words, were you planning on getting married when you were growing up? Did you see yourself as being married? Or... Excuse me. Did you just meet the right person?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't think so. Stanley and I knew each other for quite a while before we got married. And... I think we just... We just decided to get married. I mean, we... He went to Colorado and decided that that's where he wanted to be. So I went down there and we were married down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you expect in married life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've had a very happy married life. I wouldn't... I don't think I would want to change it. If I had to do it over again, I think I'd do the same thing. Because I've had a happy life. I've had two very nice children, good children. And... Out of my marriage, I've had practically everything that I've wanted. I mean, there's never been anything that... That I have... I've been well provided for. And I've been real happy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Sounds good. I... I think I've met the happiest people here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In St. Mary's? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You know, just... I haven't... This is the first place that I've been interviewed. But just this forest going out and meeting a bunch of, you know, new people. I've just found so many really happy people here. And it's nice. It really is. What effect has the number of children that you had?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well... I wanted two and I have two. I want a boy and I have a girl and that's what I have. So... And as I say, they've been real good children. I couldn't ask for better children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do for recreation now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not much. Outside of... Now I'm going to Coeur d'Alene Thursday to the State Capitol. I'm going to the convention for the American Legion. And... But I had cancer in 1967. And I've had a double mastectomy. And 167 and 169. So it limits what I can do and what I can't do. And I don't... I don't do much anymore. Other than work and enjoy myself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What sorts of recreation did you do before then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we went to a lot of the... parties at the Elks, you know. And I belonged to Mother's Club for years. And we always had parties and meetings. And I belonged to a bridge club. And I played bridge with the same group of girls for over 20 years. So, you know. And then besides raising the children and doing all the things for them. Which I had done all my life, or all their lives while they were home. I always entertained for them. When Andy graduated from high school on the night of Bacchus Laureate. I had all his class here for a party and I did the same for Candy. When she graduated from high school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you working all the time with your children before that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I started in 59.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how old was they? So they were...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Candy was about 10. I didn't work part time from 59 to about 62. I just worked, you know, part time. But then after I came back from Girl State. After I was director in the June of 62. Then I think that fall I started to work steady.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think about women working when their children are swimming?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I have mixed emotions. I never have been sorry that I was home with my children when they were little. And I was home with them. And I think every mother should be home with their children when they're small.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you mean by small?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I mean until at least they're in high school age. I think after they're up in high school, probably. Then they can do for themselves. But I think when they're little, I think they need their mothers at home. I really do. I'm not sorry that I stayed home with mine. You have lots of time to work after they're grown. And the reason I went to work was to help Andy through college. I knew that I would have to help him. And by that time Candy was big enough to more or less take care of herself. I was here after school very shortly. And then Stanley's mother lived with us at that time. And she was always here to help me with Candy. While she was through high school. But I think when they're little, I think every mother should be home with their children when they're little. I really do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you sew for them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Somewhat. Not a lot. I did some for Candy, but not a whole lot.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you teach her how to sew?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Somewhat. Not a lot. But she did a little bit of sewing, but not too much. But when she went to college, she took sewing because she took home economics. And she sews a lot now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have a garden or do you still have a garden? No. Have you ever had one? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've never had a garden.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever bought stuff to can or bring for anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. I can when the children were little and I still can. Although we don't can like we used to. I used to can a lot of, you know, fruits and things. But now the only thing we make is dill pickles. Because that's all we eat, you know. I freeze a few vegetables and can a few pears. But I don't can like I used to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does your family ever get together for recreation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Always. On Thanksgiving and Christmas we're always together.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The whole family? Uh-huh. Your son comes down? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Thanksgiving I have the family all here for dinner. Including my brothers and their families. And then for Christmas we go to my oldest brother and his family. And we're all together.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is this something you do for fun? Is this something that you developed from your family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think so, yes. My father was a great believer in having all his family together. And when we were first married and our children were small, we were together a lot on Sundays and holidays.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you do on those days?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just have dinner and visit. And spend the day together. Take pictures and things like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Didn't you mention you were in some sort of church activity?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have taught Sunday school when I was younger. And I've always sent my children to church. However, I'm not a member of the church. But we have always gone and I sent the children until they were... grown and they still go to church.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did mom use?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Growing up we went to the Presbyterian. My daughter married a Lutheran. And she goes to that church now and she's going to have her baby baptized a Lutheran. And probably join that church. And my son has always gone to the Presbyterian church. However, I don't think they attend church in Seattle right now. But when they do go, it's the Presbyterian church.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What magazines and newspapers do you subscribe to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The local paper. The Spokesman Review. And the magazines is... Better Homes and Gardens. And Family Circle. And Women's Day. And... I'll take one other one. And the Reader's Diary.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you watch television much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not as much as Stanley does. I do some, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What sorts of TV shows do you watch?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I like country and western. I like Saturday night western shows. And I sort of like all the family and that type of shows. I do watch some of them. Old MacMillan and Life, but I'm not really... I do watch some of those, but I don't like them as well as I do some of the others. And I like the Today Show. I think it's a good show.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That comes on in the morning when I get up. What are some of the most common things that your husband asks you about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know. What do you most ask me about? What? What do you most ask me about? You don't know anything, huh?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I say if you need anything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, if I need anything. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you make family decisions?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We discuss it. We discuss. If there's a problem, we discuss it and decide what to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that... I mean, when the children were growing up, was that a family thing? Was them involved? Or is it usually just between you and your husband?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If it pertained to them, we discussed it with them. If it was just something with us, we discussed it just between the two of us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that what happened when you were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think so. I think so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are some of the things that you might tell a young woman who is planning on coming to a small town or rural area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think the first thing you have to do is you have to be friendly.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Be yourself.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And be yourself, right? And you have to make friends, you know. You have to put your best foot forward to make friends. I think. You can't just remain to yourself. You have to be active. And, um, I think that's the main thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything else you'd like to tell me?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't think so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you like to tell me something else about your mother?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was a very good looking woman. She was a very stylish woman. And I know when I went to work, I did, because I was doing the depression, I would bottle out her clothes. And she always said that she always was well dressed when she was a young girl. And she had this cafe in Harrison. She made hats when she lived in Coeur d'Alene. She had a little hat shop. And then she married my father and they moved to Plummer and he, at that time, had a stull yard, which is along with the lumberjack, a stull yard. What they called stull and it was like poles today. Like a pole yard. And, um, she was a Rebecca, she joined the Rebecca Lodge. And she was a girl in Plummer. Of course, she wasn't a young girl. She was fairly old when she was married. And, um,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Go ahead.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was always a very well-liked woman. She was always a busy woman. And then she came to St. Mary's and she was active with her lodge. And, um, in fact, she was chaplain in the Rebecca Lodge here for years and years and years. That's the same as a, you know, what a chaplain is in a lodge. And she went to Grand Lodge with my sister-in-law a number of times. And she received the degree of chivalry from the Rebecca Lodge. And that's the highest honor you can get in the Rebecca Lodge. Even though...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I'll tell you. Her mother was one of the best persons you ever met. That's why I wondered. I'm interested in the idea that she was a homesteader, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then, as I said, she had this homestead from...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We weren't having any trouble. She stuck up for me. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She always took Stanley's side or my brother's wife's side. She was always... She was not biased. I mean, she knew there was two sides to every story. And then, while I was going through high school, of course, as I said, it was during the Depression time. And so she would go with the doctors here. There was three old doctors, Dr. Robbins, Dr. Cornwall, and Dr. Platt. And they would come and get her. And she would go out to these homes out of town and deliver the babies with them. And stay for two or three days with these doctors. I remember that, I thought. But she was quite a person. Real nice person. Now, is there any other questions?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, one more I thought of. How did the Depression affect your life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there was just no money. We didn't have the things in school. We barely... My brothers worked after school at odd jobs downtown. And to make their money to go to school with. And my mother, as I say, worked. But there was very few clothes. I had very few clothes. We had enough to eat. But there was none of the extra things that we ever had while I was in school. That is, in high school. And we got by, but I mean, we didn't have very much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the war affect your life during that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Only that I got married. Because I went back to Colorado and got married during the war. And... Stanley was in the infantry in Colorado. And then he was sent to Fort Lewis to guard the Germans. He never went overseas. Which I was thankful for. But I enjoyed those years. I mean, I met people. We still have friends that we knew, that we met when he was in the Army. And we correspond with them once a year at Christmas time. We have had a couple come to visit us. But it's been a number of years. We had a family from Michigan that stopped one time to see us that we knew when we were in the service. And we had another couple come from California that we knew.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That came to see us.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I might say that the year that Stanley was at Fort Lewis, Andy was picked as... Let's see, he was probably about two and a half. And they picked Stanley for their paper that they published at Fort Lewis as the father of the year. And they printed his picture with Andy. And it went all over the world as father of the year. And Andy was the little boy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We still have the picture. Oh, wow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They have a lot of them all the pictures. Well, I know. But it was such a nice honor for both Stanley and Andy. Now are there any other questions?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My question is more than a minute ago. Have you traveled very much aside from Chicago?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My oldest brother is a Ford dealer. And I have been to San Francisco to a car showing. And I've been to Las Vegas to a car showing with him. And we've been to Reno several times. And of course now that Andy lives in Seattle, we go over there two or three times a year.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever been outside the United States? No. Have you ever headed to Georgia?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I've been up to Canada. Well, yeah, up to Canada. But then I don't even think about that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you been to the United States?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Huh? No, I haven't been to the United States. Well, yeah, I've been up to Canada.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you're in Idaho it is. When you're in Georgia it is. You're like the kid. I'm like the kid.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Have you been up to Idaho? Oh, yeah, we've been up to Canada. We went up fishing a couple times. Well, we were back in Michigan too. I forgot about that. When the kids were little we went back to Michigan one time on a trip.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do for vacation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, since I've been working, I just take a few days at a time. But we usually go over to Andy's. And then we have a present that is in southern Idaho. And we go down to Boise. In the Boise area. He lives down there. We've been down there. And then as I say, a couple of vacations I took. I went with my brother because Stanley couldn't get away. So I went to Las Vegas. They would be fun to interview because they've been to Europe and the San Juan Islands on Ford trips. You know, Ford people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But they're in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They live here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, they live here? Mm-hmm. Is there anything else you can think of? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think that about covered everything.
